title: Could Paying Attention to Pain Help You Heal
paragraphs: When people are injured or in pain, they often try to distract themselves, for example by watching TV or listening to music. However, a new study from Israel suggests that paying close attention to an injury may actually help the body's natural healing process.

The study was carried out by a team of scientists including Liron Rozenkrantz, a neuroscientist at Bar-Ilan University, and the results were published in 2026. The researchers worked with a small group of healthy people. To cause a mild inflammation, they pricked the participants' skin with histamine, a substance that the body releases during allergic reactions. This produced swelling and redness.

Next, some of the participants were asked to pay close attention to the inflamed area for about 20 minutes. The others were asked to distract themselves. Importantly, the participants were not told what to expect, and no one was deceived.

The researchers found that the body's response to the inflammation worked better when people focused on it. According to reports, nearly 90% of participants had less inflammation when they paid attention to it, and the total swelling and redness was about one and a half times smaller than when they were distracted.

Rozenkrantz explained that signals from inflamed areas reach the brain whether people pay attention to them or not. However, paying attention appears to help the brain control the body's immune response more efficiently. Rozenkrantz also pointed out that this effect is different from the placebo effect, which depends on people having certain expectations.

However, the study had some important limitations. It only tested one type of inflammation, caused by small skin pricks, in healthy people. The participants did not have any chronic pain or illness. In addition, very severe pain cannot be studied in a laboratory, and in such cases, distraction may still be helpful.

Rozenkrantz stressed that people should not stop taking painkillers based on these results. More research will be needed to find out whether the effect could help with other types of injuries, such as surgical wounds.
